function.name: requests_get

message.content:
Below are two common ways to pull *detailed* information for a specific interface on a network device: | Method | What you’ll see | Typical command / API call | Notes | |--------|-----------------|---------------------------|-------| | **CLI** | All operational & configuration data (status, speed, duplex, MTU, errors, counters, description, etc.) | `show interface `
`show interfaces detail`
`show running-config interface ` | Works on most vendor OSes (Cisco IOS/IOS‑XE, Juniper JUNOS, Arista EOS, etc.). The exact syntax may vary slightly. | | **REST API** | Same data returned in JSON (or XML) format, optionally filtered to only the fields you care about | `GET https://api.example.com/devices/{device_id}/interfaces/{interface_id}`
Optional query: `?fields=all` or `?fields=status,speed,description,counters` | Requires that the device is managed by a controller that exposes an API (e.g., Cisco DNA Center, Juniper Contrail, Arista CloudVision). | --- ### 1. Using the CLI ```bash # Example on a Cisco IOS router router# show interface GigabitEthernet0/1 GigabitEthernet0/1 is up, line protocol is up Hardware is Gigabit Ethernet, address is 00c0.29ff.1234 (bia 00c0.29ff.1234) Description: Uplink to core switch MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec ... Internet address is 192.168.1.1/24 ... ``` If you want *all* available details in one shot: ```bash router# show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/1 detail ``` On Juniper devices: ```bash user@router> show interfaces ge-0/0/1 detail ``` On Arista EOS: ```bash Arista# show interface Ethernet1 detail ``` --- ### 2. Using the REST API Assuming your controller exposes a `/devices/{device_id}/interfaces/{interface_id}` endpoint, you can fetch the data with a simple HTTP GET. Here’s a quick example using the `requests_get` helper defined in the toolset: ```python from functions import requests_get # Replace with your actual device ID and interface name device_id = "12345" interface_name = "GigabitEthernet0/1" url = f"https://api.example.com/devices/{device_id}/interfaces/{interface_name}" # If you only want a subset of fields: params = {"fields": "status,speed,description,counters"} response = requests_get({"url": url, "params": params}) print(response.json()) ``` The response will look something like this (JSON): ```json { "name": "GigabitEthernet0/1", "status": "up", "line_protocol": "up", "speed": "1000Mbps", "duplex": "full", "mtu": 1500, "description": "Uplink to core switch", "counters": { "in_octets": 123456789, "out_octets": 987654321, "in_errors": 0, "out_errors": 0 }, "ip_address": "192.168.1.1/24", ... } ``` If your controller supports filtering, you can reduce payload size by specifying only the fields you need: ```python params = {"fields": "name,status,description"} ``` --- #### Quick Checklist - **Do you have CLI access?** - Yes → Use `show interface …` or `show interfaces … detail`. - No → Use the API route above. - **Do you need the data in a machine‑readable format?** - Yes → Prefer the REST API. - No → CLI output is fine; you can copy/paste into a spreadsheet or log file. - **Do you want to automate this?** - Use the `requests_get` function (or any HTTP client) to script the API call. - For CLI automation, consider SSH libraries (`paramiko`, `netmiko`) or network automation frameworks (`napalm`, `pyATS`). Feel free to let me know which platform you’re working on (Cisco, Juniper, Arista, etc.) and I can give you the exact command syntax or API path for that vendor!
